title: American Dreamz
full_review:
The "American Idol" phenomenon gets a good skewering in "American Dreamz" (Universal). Then again, so does George Bush. So, too, does America's role in the Middle East.

There are, in fact, probably too many targets in this latest film from director-writer Paul Weitz, but this is on the whole an amusing satire of fame and politics, despite some elements that on paper might raise eyebrows.

First, there's a would-be terrorist, Omer (Sam Golzari), who's more enamored of American show tunes than suicide missions, so he's sent from somewhere near the Pakistan-Afghanistan border to stay with his unsuspecting Arab-American cousins in California.

Then there's Sally (Mandy Moore), a small-town Ohio singer wannabe pushed by her mother (Jennifer Coolidge) to land a spot on the "American Dreamz" TV show, while the girl's boring suitor William (Chris Klein), who, upon being rejected by her, enlists for the Iraq War and is wounded by a stray bullet before he even sees combat.

Martin Tweed (Hugh Grant) is the Simon Cowell-like host who, in his quest for novel talent, sets his sights on recruiting the opportunistic Sally, whose "white trash" persona and "war hero" boyfriend will win viewers' hearts, and also decides that an Arabic contestant would be a ratings-grabber.

Tweed's scouts mistake Omer for his cousin -- previously failed applicant Iqbal (a very funny Tony Yalda) -- and hire him for the show.

And finally, there's the Bush-like President Staton (Dennis Quaid), who spends his days in bed reading the newspapers, and allows his chief of staff (Willem Dafoe in a Dick Cheney get-up) to do his talking (and thinking). Marcia Gay Harden as the first lady strongly suggests Laura Bush.

When Omer's superiors learn their hapless charge is to go on the popular show, they set him up to kill Staton, who is appearing as a celebrity judge. Meanwhile, much to his amazement, the cynical Tweed finds himself falling for Sally.

Weitz carefully avoids most of the bad-taste pitfalls, but some may still find the terrorist business insensitive fodder for comedy. With memories of the perpetrators of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks so vivid, it's difficult to view them as humorous one-dimensional villains, the way Russians used to turn up in movies as bad guys. But Weitz also underscores the paradox of how those who set out to destroy American culture can be smitten with it. On the other hand, the moderate portrayal of Omer's relatives is one of the screen's more positive depictions of Arab-Americans.

So, too, Bush barbs are softened both by Quaid's very human performance and the ultimate transformation of his character, which we won't spoil.

By the time this black comedy winds up, it's clear that there are no real "bad guys" here, and there's a commendable message about the vapidity of today's pop culture, the public's misplaced priorities, the need for understanding of our "enemies," and the obscenity of war.

The salvos could perhaps have been more sharply focused, but if they had, the film might have lost some of its low-keyed charm, which, as it is, has more comic muscle than Albert Brooks' recent "Looking for Comedy in the Muslim World."

The film contains scattered instances of four-letter words, profanity, and sexual and crass expressions, an implied premarital coupling and a suicide. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
